description:
Their behavior is telling you the truth.

If someone’s actions show you that your needs aren’t a priority, believe them. That’s the “Let Them” part.

But then comes the harder piece: “Let Me.” Let me ask myself, “Is this behavior what I deserve? Is this what I’m willing to accept?”

Because here’s the thing: people only change when they want to or when they can. And if you’ve clearly asked for what you need and they still won’t step up, then you’re left with a choice.

You can’t keep clinging to the fantasy of who you wish someone would be while ignoring who they’re showing you they really are.

Listen to this full conversation with @jayshetty on the @jayshettypodcast 🎧 "Mel Robbins: How to Use the ‘Let Them Theory’ (A Life Changing Mindset Hack That 15 Million People Can’t Stop Talking About)"
transcript: their behavior is telling you the truth. Their behavior is telling you what they care about and what their priorities are. And if their behavior is telling you that your needs are not a priority, you have to let them reveal that. That's also what let them means. Yes. Because then you're going to come back to the second part, which is, let me ask myself, is this kind of behavior from somebody what I deserve? Is this what I'm willing to accept in somebody? Because again, what do we also know? People only change when they want to or they can. And you might be in a situation where somebody would really love to change, but they can't because they're dealing with some challenge right now, or they don't have the skill yet. And you may decide if that's the case to still love and accept the person. Right. Right. Yeah. But there may be times where you have had the conversation and it is very clear they're capable of it. They just won't do it. Yeah. And what I find in relationships where that sort of invisible distance and the frustration and the resentment comes up is twofold. Number one, you can't detach from your emotions and say, let them and really fully just let the person be who they are. And you don't do the part, let me, where you actually take responsibility for expressing in a mature way what you need and how their behavior impacts you. And so if you don't ever express what you need and how it's impacting you, you're not actually giving somebody the opportunity to build a skill or to change or to love you the way that you need them to love you so that you feel loved. The second mistake that I see constantly is that you make the ask and then the person doesn't do it. And then you start making excuses and resentment builds and you stay in something, seeing exactly who someone is, wishing they would change, living up here in your mind about the fantasy of what you wish this was, refusing to accept the reality of what it actually is.
